svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Key distribution, as taught and as it actually works now
svg.desc: Two panels. The left panel describes the web of trust model that most guides still teach: verify a key, sign it, upload the signature to a keyserver, and let trust propagate through mutual acquaintances. The right panel explains why that no longer functions: the old keyserver network was attacked in 2019 by attaching enormous numbers of signatures to certificates, and the recommended replacement keyserver deliberately does not distribute third-party signatures at all. It then lists what is used in practice instead.
svg.text: Figure 3: The Web of Trust Does Not Propagate Any More
Most guides still teach the left panel. The recommended keyserver removes the very thing the left panel depends on.

g.text: 1. You verify a fingerprint in person
and confirm the key belongs to them.
2. You sign their key
which attaches your signature to their certificate as
a public statement that you checked.
3. You upload the signed key
so that everybody else can see your endorsement.
4. Trust propagates
Somebody who trusts you can now extend some trust
to them, through you, without meeting them.

svg.text: WHY STEPS 3 AND 4 NO LONGER WORK

g.text: The old keyserver network was attacked in 2019
Nothing in the format limits how many signatures a
certificate may carry. Two well-known contributors had
tens of thousands attached to theirs. Importing a
poisoned certificate could disable a local installation.
The network was append-only, so nothing could be removed.
The replacement keyserver strips them deliberately
The keyserver now recommended everywhere does not
distribute third-party signatures at all, precisely because
they let anybody attach unlimited data to anybody's key.
So your signature on their key is not delivered to anyone.

svg.text: What is actually used to obtain a key now

g.text: Directly from the person
over a channel you already trust, which is what you were verifying against anyway.
From their own domain
through the directory mechanism a mail client can query automatically, which ties the key to control of the address.
From a keyserver that verifies the address
by mailing a confirmation before publishing, so the listing means something.
From a published fingerprint
on a site you have independent reason to trust, checked against what you downloaded.

svg.text: Verifying a fingerprint is still correct and still necessary. What stopped working is the idea that your verification helps anybody else.
Verify for yourself. Do not expect a trust network to carry it onward, because there is no longer one carrying it.
